title: GitHub Flow
description: Use the GitHub Flow model: short-lived branches, pull requests, and deploy-to-main for continuous delivery.

data.text: GitHub Flow is a lightweight branching strategy optimized for continuous deployment. It has a single long-lived main branch, short-lived feature branches, and pull requests as the integration point. It is the simplest Git workflow and the natural choice for teams that deploy frequently.

data.title: Core principles
items: **main is always deployable** — Anything on main has been reviewed and passes CI
**Feature branches for everything** — Branch off main for any change, bug fix, or experiment
**Pull request before merge** — Open a PR, get review, pass CI, then merge
**Merge and deploy immediately** — After merging, deploy to production right away

data.title: GitHub Flow end-to-end
data.code:
# Step 1: Create a branch from main
git switch -c feature/update-header main

# Step 2: Make changes and commit
git add .
git commit -m "feat(ui): update page header"

# Step 3: Push and open a pull request
git push -u origin feature/update-header
# Open PR on GitHub for review

# Step 4: After review and CI pass, merge via GitHub UI
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Step 5: Delete the feature branch
git branch -d feature/update-header

git push origin --delete feature/update-header

data.title: Use feature flags with GitHub Flow
data.text: GitHub Flow works best when you can deploy incomplete features safely. Feature flags let you merge code to main before it is user-facing, decoupling deploy from release.
The pull request as a quality gate

Pull requests are the integration point in GitHub Flow. They enable code review, automated testing, and discussion before changes reach main. Requiring at least one approval and passing CI before merge creates a strong quality gate.
With GitHub Flow, every merge to main is a potential production deployment. Typical setups have a staging environment that mirrors production and a production deploy triggered by merging to main.

items: **Production deploy** — Triggered by tag or environment promotion from staging
Teams with strong automated testing and CI/CD pipelines
Small-to-medium teams comfortable with rapid iteration
Mobile apps with long review cycles (App Store, Google Play)
Teams that need a formal stabilization period before release
Projects with complex multi-service integration requirements

items.question: Does GitHub Flow require GitHub?
items.answer: No. The model can be implemented with any Git hosting platform that supports pull or merge requests (GitLab, Bitbucket, etc.).

items.question: Can I use GitHub Flow with trunk-based development?
items.answer: Yes. GitHub Flow and trunk-based development share the same main-branch philosophy. Trunk-based is often considered a superset of GitHub Flow.

items.question: How do I handle database migrations in GitHub Flow?
items.answer: Use backward-compatible migrations that do not break the old code. Deploy the schema change first, then deploy the code change.

items.question: What if my main branch has a bug?
items.answer: Fix it directly on main with a hotfix branch, or revert the bad commit with git revert. The key is that main is always deployable — fix issues immediately.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: GitHub Flow uses a single long-lived main branch
Every change goes through a feature branch and pull request
Main is always deployable; merge and deploy immediately
Pair with feature flags for incomplete-feature safety
Ideal for continuous deployment teams with strong CI/CD
